absent: Pack and unpack implementation, bit numbering, quirk semantics beyond test vectors, and error conditions.
Parman operations, priority, and item structure layouts, move and resize contracts, and concurrency rules.
Parser table and substring layouts, maximum argument bound value, and numeric helper contracts.
Per-CPU reference structure layouts, flag bit positions, get and put and switch and reinit operations, and release callback contract.
KUnit helper semantics and parameter generator behavior.

findings.text: Manager state holds an operations pointer, a private context pointer, an algorithm pointer, a live count, a capacity limit, and a priority list. Algorithm state holds add and remove hooks. The available algorithm table provides a linear sorted implementation.

Capacity grows by one resize step through the operations resize hook and commits the new limit only on success while propagating failure. Shrinking computes limit minus one step, leaves state unchanged when the result would fall below the configured base, otherwise attempts resize and commits only on success.
A priority counts as used exactly when its item list is non-empty. Edge helpers expose the first and last entries of that list and the index values stored in those entries.

Linear ordering keeps indices dense in priority order. A new index is one past the last index of the nearest used priority at or below the target, else zero. Downward shift relocates the first entry of a priority after its last entry; upward shift relocates the last entry before its first entry; each relocation uses the move hook for one entry, relinks the list, and refreshes the stored index. Same-priority removal deletes the last entry directly or swaps the last entry into the removed slot. Addition enlarges when full, shifts lower priorities down, appends with the computed index, and increments the count. Removal compacts within the priority, shifts higher priorities up, decrements the count, and shrinks when spare capacity reaches one step.

Lifecycle interface creates a manager from operations and private context with limit seeded from base count and algorithm selected through operations, destroys a manager, initializes and finalizes priority handles with sorted insertion by numeric priority, and adds or removes items by delegating to the selected algorithm.
Destroying a manager whose priority list is non-empty and finalizing a priority that still holds items each follow a warning path. Callers must drain those lists first.

Tests use a tightly packed eight byte buffer type, a mixed-width record with one 32 bit member plus three 16 bit members plus two 8 bit members, and a descriptor table that partitions a 64 bit span into six contiguous ranges assigned to those members from most significant to least significant.

Single-value vectors exercise two distinct magic 64 bit patterns and an all-ones pattern at aligned and odd bit positions inside otherwise zeroed buffers of several lengths, covering the no-quirk case as well as least-significant-word-first and little-endian-word and most-significant-bit-on-right adjustments alone and in combination, each case supplying value plus start and end bit positions plus quirks plus expected bytes.

Parameterized single-value checks cover packing and unpacking. Packing allocates a zeroed buffer sized per case, invokes packing with value and bit range and size and quirks, then requires success and byte equality. Unpacking reuses the stored buffer, invokes unpacking with the same range description, then requires success and value equality. Both are registered as parameterized cases in a common suite.

Multi-field checks cover packing a fixed record into an eight byte buffer with full-buffer comparison against an expected byte sequence, and unpacking a fixed byte sequence into a zeroed record with per-field comparison against expected numeric results. Both are registered alongside the single-value checks under one suite name terminated by an empty entry.
Multi-field buffer size fact is eight bytes.

Pattern matching treats an absent pattern as a match, otherwise compares literal segments and interprets conversions. Double percent matches one literal percent. String conversion requires non-empty remainder and honors an optional decimal length limit. Numeric conversions accept signed, unsigned, octal, and hexadecimal forms and require that at least one character converts. Captured slices are recorded in order subject to a maximum argument bound, and mismatch or unsupported conversion yields no match.
Token lookup scans a table in order until one pattern matches the input and returns the token associated with that entry, forwarding a caller-provided capture array.

Signed conversion copies the captured slice into a bounded temporary buffer, reports range error when the slice does not fit, parses with a caller-selected base, reports invalid when nothing converts, reports range error when the result falls outside signed integer limits, otherwise stores the narrowed result and reports success. Thin wrappers fix the base to automatic, octal, or hexadecimal.

Sixty-four bit and unsigned conversions share bounded copying with truncation reported as range error, then delegate to kernel string-to-integer helpers with automatic base for sixty-four bit and decimal base for unsigned, propagating helper status and storing the value only on success.
Public parser helpers expose token matching, bounded slice copying, slice duplication, and integer conversions across several widths and bases.
Slice copying reports the full distance between slice bounds, copies at most size minus one bytes when size is non-zero, and terminates the destination in that case.
Slice duplication allocates a terminated copy holding exactly the bytes between the slice bounds using kernel allocation.
Numeric conversion temporary buffer length fact is twenty four bytes.
Per-CPU bias fact is one shifted to the top bit of an unsigned long, reserving the high bit to distinguish per-CPU mode counts.
Logging prefix combines the current function name with the supplied format.
Counter accessor recovers the per-CPU pointer by clearing low flag bits that share the same word.
Reference lifecycle exposes initialization with a release callback plus flags plus allocation mode, and a teardown that releases per-CPU storage and auxiliary data.

Lifecycle moves among live per-CPU, live atomic, dead, and exiting states. Initialization selects atomic mode when atomic or dead start is requested and otherwise starts per-CPU with bias plus one live reference. Dead start sets the dead flag without the live increment. Exit frees per-CPU storage when present and marks combined atomic-dead, then folds any remaining atomic count into the shared word and drops auxiliary data, with absent data causing early return after storage release.
Teardown serializes folding the auxiliary count into the shared pointer word and clearing the data pointer under an interrupt-saving spin lock.

Initialization can fail for lack of memory at either allocation step, releasing partial per-CPU storage and zeroing its handle when the second allocation fails. Teardown warns when a mode switch is still in progress as indicated by a pending confirmation hook.

Initialization aligns per-CPU storage to cover flag bits and pointer alignment, derives forced-atomic and reinit permissions from flags while forcing reinit permission when starting atomic or dead, and records the release hook with no pending switch confirmation plus a back link to the reference.
